title: Reasons for Having a Low CIBIL Score & How to Improve It?
summary: Late payments, high card use, many applications and settled loans can lower your CIBIL score. See what to change and how long it takes to show.
body_markdown:
A CIBIL score is usually low because of something recorded in your credit report, the record lenders send a bureau of your loans and card payments. It may be late or missed payments, heavy use of your card limits or several recent loan applications. A settled account, a loan you stood guarantor for going bad, or too little history to score can also do it. Improving it means changing what lenders report about you. Since July 2026 lenders send that data four times a month, so a change should reach your report within about two weeks.


How far the score moves after that, no bureau publishes. Nothing raises it overnight.


## Why is your CIBIL score low?


Your CIBIL score is worked out from the accounts and the enquiries in your credit report, so a low score points back to something recorded there. CIBIL is TransUnion CIBIL, one of four credit bureaus in India. A credit bureau is a company registered with RBI that keeps credit records and produces your credit report and score. Your credit report is the record lenders send a bureau of your loans and card payments. A credit score is a three-digit number, from 300 to 900, that a bureau works out from that report. The same habits move every bureau's score.


How a score is calculated, and what goes into it, is in[the credit score article](https://koshex.com/blog/credit-score) .


The reasons recorded behind a low score are these:


- Payments made late or missed, covered in the next section.
- A large share of your card limits in use, covered under utilisation.
- Many loan or card applications in a short time.
- A loan that was settled for less than you owed.
- No loan or card yet, so the bureau has little to go on.


One cause surprises people. If you stood guarantor on someone's loan, or took a loan jointly, a default by the main borrower can lower your score too. A guarantor is a person who agrees to repay if the borrower does not. A co-borrower shares the loan with the main borrower. CIBIL says a guarantor is equally responsible.


If the score dropped and you cannot see why, open your report and look for an account, an enquiry or a late mark you do not recognise. A wrong entry can be disputed. The steps are in[the credit score article](https://koshex.com/blog/credit-score) .


## How do late or missed payments affect your score?


A payment made after its due date makes the loan overdue from that day, and lenders pass days past due to the bureaus at their next reporting date. Days past due (DPD) is the number of days a payment has stayed unpaid. Under RBI's rules, any amount due to a bank is treated as overdue if it is not paid on the due date.


Banks tag the account as it ages. Up to 30 days overdue it is an early-stress account (SMA-0), 31 to 60 days is SMA-1, and 61 to 90 days is SMA-2. RBI applies these stages to all loans other than farm loans, retail loans included. If an instalment stays unpaid for more than 90 days on a term loan, the loan becomes a non-performing asset (NPA) in the bank's books, which shows on your credit report. An EMI, the equated monthly instalment, is the fixed amount you pay each month that covers interest and part of the loan.


When a lender sends default or days-past-due information to the bureaus, RBI's rules require it to alert you by SMS or email.


Credit cards have a small allowance. A card account is reported as past due to the bureaus only when it stays past due for more than three days, counted from the due date.


What a missed EMI costs beyond the credit report, such as penal charges, is in[what are EMIs and how do they work](https://koshex.com/blog/what-are-emis-and-how-do-they-work) . If you are already struggling to pay,[the debt trap article](https://koshex.com/blog/5-steps-to-get-out-of-a-debt-trap) covers what to do.


## What is credit utilisation, and why does it matter?


Credit utilisation is the share of your credit card limits that you are using. A card limit is the most the card issuer lets you spend on that card. Bureaus count utilisation: CIBIL's steps include "Keep your balances low ... control your utilization", and CRIF High Mark lists the utilisation ratio in revolving credit among its factors.


Here is the arithmetic with an illustration. Karthik is a 27-year-old software tester in Hyderabad with two cards, limits of ₹60,000 and ₹90,000. His total limit is ₹1,50,000.


Balance reported Share of the ₹1,50,000 limit used


One month ₹96,000 64%


After paying down ₹30,000 20%


Same person, same cards, same limits. Only the share used changed. The balance that counts is the one your card issuer reports to the bureaus.


No bureau publishes a safe percentage, so there is no figure to aim for. CIBIL's own words are "Keep your balances low". Paying a bill in full and on time is one thing, and using only a small part of the limit is another. CIBIL lists both as separate steps.


## Do loan applications lower your score?


Each application lets the lender look at your credit report, and Experian says a hard enquiry can lower your score for a while. Experian calls a lender's check when you apply a hard enquiry. CIBIL explains it this way: every time you apply for a loan or credit card, the bank or institution accesses your report, and the system notes it in your credit history as an enquiry. A rejection is a different matter. RBI's rules say information about loans declined previously shall not be reported by a credit bureau. The rejection itself never reaches your report. The enquiry that came with the application does, and many applications in a short time add many enquiries.


CIBIL's advice is to apply for new credit in moderation. If a lender has already turned you down,[why personal loans get rejected](https://koshex.com/blog/common-reasons-for-personal-loan-rejection-tips-to-avoid) covers what to do next.


## What does a settled or written-off account do to your score?


A settled account tells lenders you paid less than you owed, and lenders read it as a warning. "Settled" means the lender accepted less than you owed because you could not pay in full. RBI lets lenders use that status only where, because of financial inability to repay on the original terms, a principal or interest waiver, or both, was given. "Closed" means you paid everything.


A CIBIL blog case shows the difference. A borrower paid less than the full amount and the loan was reported as "settled"; had he paid everything, it would have shown "closed". CIBIL notes that lenders view "settled" as risky.


A bank that settles with you must also wait before lending to you again. RBI requires a cooling period set by the bank's board-approved policy, of at least 12 months, except for farm loans. A compromise settlement, in RBI's words, is a negotiated arrangement to fully settle the bank's claims in cash, and it may involve some sacrifice of the amount due.


### Can you improve your score after a settlement?


Paying the remaining balance can turn "settled" into "closed". In CIBIL's example, the borrower paid the rest, got the no-objection certificate from the lender, raised a dispute, and the status changed from "settled" to "closed" within 30 days. That is one case CIBIL describes, not a promise for every account.


Closing or settling a loan does not wipe it off your report. Closed accounts stay on it as history, and RBI's 2006 regulations make bureaus keep credit information for a minimum of seven years. No rule says exactly when an old account must drop off.


### What are a technical write-off and wilful default?


A technical write-off is when the bank removes a non-performing loan from its books for accounting only, without giving up its claim on you. The money is still owed.


Wilful default is a narrower term than people assume. RBI treats a default as wilful when the borrower could pay but did not, diverted the money, or sold the security without the lender's approval. The "wilful defaulter" label applies when ₹25 lakh or more is outstanding. Missing EMIs because money is short is not wilful default.


## What if you have no credit history?


With no loan or card yet, a bureau may have nothing to score, and that is not a bad score. CIBIL calls it a "No Hit": based on the details submitted, there is not enough credit activity to generate a CIBIL score and report.


RBI tells banks that first-time borrowers' loan applications should not be rejected just because they have no credit history. What lenders look at instead is in[how to get a personal loan with a low CIBIL score](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-get-a-personal-loan-for-a-low-cibil-score) .


A loan against a fixed deposit or against mutual funds is reported like any other loan. Missed interest payments can hurt the score the same way. See[loans against fixed deposits](https://koshex.com/blog/do-banks-offer-loans-against-fixed-deposits) and[loans against mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/get-loan-against-mutual-funds) .


## How can you improve your CIBIL score?


You improve a score by changing what lenders report: paying on time, keeping balances low, borrowing only when needed and watching loans you stand guarantor for. Most of these are CIBIL's own steps:


1. **Pay every EMI and card bill on time.** CIBIL's first step is "Always pay your dues on time". An auto-debit instruction from your bank account is one practical way to avoid a missed date.
2. **Clear overdue amounts first.** Lenders report accounts whose days past due have changed, so the change appears at the lender's next reporting date.
3. **Bring card balances down.** CIBIL: "Keep your balances low".
4. **Apply for new credit in moderation.** Each application adds an enquiry.
5. **Keep an eye on joint accounts and loans you back.** CIBIL asks you to monitor accounts you co-signed, hold jointly or stand guarantor for, every month.
6. **Review your report and dispute wrong entries.** The route is in[the credit score article](https://koshex.com/blog/credit-score) .


CIBIL also mentions a healthy mix of credit. It means secured loans such as a home or auto loan, and unsecured ones such as personal loans and cards. Too many unsecured loans, it adds, may be viewed negatively.


## How long does it take to improve a CIBIL score?


There is no fixed time. Lenders send updates to the bureaus four times a month, with data as on the 9th, 16th, 23rd and the last day. A payment you make should normally reach your report within about two weeks.


RBI's rules say no repayment, including the last instalment, may be left unreported. A worked example of the update timing is in[the credit score article](https://koshex.com/blog/credit-score) .


What no bureau publishes is how far or how fast the score then moves.


If your score has not risen after you repaid, the next reporting date may not have passed. Look at the next update, then at the report itself to confirm the lender has shown the payment. If it has not, dispute the entry.
